items.stem: The trade at Tidore described in the excerpt best illustrates which of the following developments of the period from 1450 to 1750?

options.text: Iberian efforts to reach Asian spice sources directly by sea
options.label: key
options.why: Magellan's fleet sailed for Castile to reach the Moluccas by a western sea route and bought cloves directly from the King of Tidore. Like Portugal's earlier Indian Ocean voyages, it aimed to get around the middlemen who controlled the overland and Mediterranean spice routes.

options.text: Chartered joint-stock companies taking control of the Indonesian clove trade
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Dutch East India Company was founded in 1602 and took over the clove trade later in the 1600s. The 1521 fleet was a royal Castilian expedition, not a company venture.

options.text: The transfer of American food crops to Asian farming regions through Pacific trade
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The excerpt is about cloth and knives traded for cloves, not crop transfers. Regular trans-Pacific exchange began only with the Manila galleons after 1565.

options.text: European conquest of large inland territories across mainland Southeast Asia
options.label: overstated
options.why: The excerpt shows Europeans bargaining with local kings and depending on their goodwill. Europeans at this time held only scattered coastal posts and did not rule large inland territories.

facts: Magellan's expedition left Spain in 1519 under the Castilian crown and reached the Moluccas in 1521.
The surviving ship Victoria returned to Spain in 1522, completing the first circumnavigation.
The Dutch East India Company was founded in 1602.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The fleet negotiates with the King of Tidore for a cargo of cloves after sailing from Seville, which shows a European state seeking direct access to spices.
design.evidence_quote: there they treated with the King for their cargo, and the King engaged to give them a cargo

items.stem: The pilot carefully records how many ells of cloth and how many knives bought each bahar of cloves. This focus most likely reflects that

options.text: the expedition aimed to bring spices back to Castile at a profit
options.label: key
options.why: The pilot gives exact rates of exchange and the value of the cloth in Castile. That fits a voyage sent to bring back profitable cloves, which were valuable in European markets.

options.text: the fleet was sent mainly to convert the rulers of Maluku to Christianity
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Religion is never mentioned in the excerpt. The pilot's attention is on prices and cargo, not on conversion.

options.text: Castile hoped to sell American silver for Asian spices in Maluku markets
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The fleet paid in cloth and knives. Large flows of American silver into Asia began after the Potosi strike of 1545 and the Manila galleon trade.

options.text: European cloth was more valued in Maluku than in any other Asian market
options.label: overstated
options.why: The excerpt gives prices only at Tidore and makes no comparison with other Asian markets.

facts: Cloves grew in the Moluccas and were among the most valuable spices in European trade in the early 1500s.
Silver from Potosi, discovered in 1545, later became a major means of paying for Asian goods.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The pilot lists exact amounts of cloth and knives per bahar and notes what the cloth was worth in Castile, which shows a commercial purpose.
design.evidence_quote: fourteen ells of yellow cloth of twenty-seven tem, which are worth in Castile a ducat the ell

items.stem: Which detail from the excerpt would best support a historian's argument that local rulers in Maluku shaped the terms of their contact with Europeans?

options.text: The Portuguese man could not meet the fleet without the king's permission
options.label: key
options.why: The Portuguese man said he did not dare to come because the local king forbade it, and he came only once the king allowed it. This shows a Maluku ruler controlling contact between Europeans.

options.text: Yellow cloth given for cloves was worth about a ducat per ell in Castile
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This detail is in the excerpt, but it describes the value of goods in Castile. It says nothing about the power of local rulers.

options.text: The author notes that a European fortress now stood on the island of Targatell
options.label: reversal
options.why: A fortress points to growing European power in the islands, which cuts against the argument rather than supporting it.

options.text: The captains refused the cloves of Baraham unless its king delivered them in person
options.label: reversal
options.why: Here the European captains set the conditions, so the detail shows European rather than local control over the terms.

facts: In the early 1500s, rival sultanates such as Ternate and Tidore controlled clove production in the Moluccas.
Portugal built a fortress on Ternate in 1522.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The Portuguese man refused to meet the fleet until the local king gave permission.
design.evidence_quote: he answered that he did not dare, because the King of the country forbade it

items.stem: Which of the following developments most directly explains why a Portuguese man was already living near Tidore when Magellan's fleet arrived in 1521?

options.text: Portugal's seizure of Malacca in 1511 and push into Asian sea trade
options.label: key
options.why: After Portugal took Malacca in 1511, Portuguese ships went on to the Moluccas. That explains why a Portuguese man was on a nearby island before the Castilians arrived.

options.text: The Treaty of Zaragoza of 1529 assigning the Spice Islands to Portugal
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The treaty came eight years after 1521, so it cannot explain a Portuguese presence already there that year.

options.text: The Dutch East India Company's capture of Portuguese posts in the islands
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Dutch seized Portuguese posts in the Moluccas in the 1600s, long after 1521.

options.text: The Ming treasure fleets that carried Chinese envoys to Southeast Asian ports
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Zheng He's voyages ended in 1433. They were Chinese ventures and have no connection to the Portuguese presence in Maluku.

facts: Portugal captured Malacca in 1511.
Portuguese ships reached the Moluccas soon after the capture of Malacca, by about 1512.
Zheng He's last voyage ended in 1433.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt says a Portuguese man was already the chief person on a nearby island in 1521, which points students to earlier Portuguese expansion into Asian waters.
design.evidence_quote: in another island near, there was a Portuguese man

items.stem: In the decade after the voyage, the competing Castilian and Portuguese claims to Maluku cloves seen in the excerpt were most directly settled by which agreement?

options.text: The Treaty of Zaragoza, in which Castile gave up its claim to the islands
options.label: key
options.why: The excerpt shows Castile and Portugal competing over the same cloves and the same local rulers. In the Treaty of Zaragoza (1529), Charles V gave up Castile's claim to the Moluccas in return for a Portuguese payment.

options.text: The Treaty of Tordesillas, which first divided newly found lands between the two crowns
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Tordesillas was signed in 1494, before the voyage. Its line did not settle which crown owned the Moluccas on the other side of the world, which is why a dispute arose.

options.text: The Iberian Union, which placed Portugal under the Spanish king from 1580
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The union came half a century later, after a succession crisis in Portugal, and it was not a settlement of the clove dispute.

options.text: The Peace of Westphalia, which ended religious wars among European states
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) ended the Thirty Years' War and had nothing to do with Iberian claims in Asia.

facts: The Treaty of Zaragoza (1529) gave Portugal the Moluccas in exchange for a payment to Charles V.
The Treaty of Tordesillas was signed in 1494.
The Iberian Union began in 1580.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The King of Baraham had sold cloves to Portugal but offered them to the Castilians and asked to become a vassal of Castile, which shows the rival Iberian claims.
design.evidence_quote: he wished to be a vassal of the King of Castile

items.stem: Because the account was written by a pilot sailing in Magellan's fleet, it is most limited as a source for understanding

options.text: how the people of Tidore viewed the bargains made with the fleet
options.label: key
options.why: The account gives only the fleet's side of the deal. It reports what the local king agreed to, but not how Tidore's rulers or people judged the exchange.

options.text: the kinds of trade goods the fleet offered in exchange for cloves
options.label: reversal
options.why: A member of the fleet would know exactly what goods were offered, and the excerpt lists the cloth and knives. This is a strength of the source, not a limit.

options.text: the units of weight and measure used in buying and selling the spice
options.label: reversal
options.why: The pilot records the bahar and the ell directly, so the source is useful for trade measures rather than limited on them.

options.text: the presence of Portuguese traders in Maluku before Castilian ships arrived
options.label: reversal
options.why: The fleet's members met the Portuguese man in person, so the account is direct testimony about the Portuguese presence.

facts: Magellan's fleet reached Tidore in November 1521.
Tidore was ruled by a sultan who traded cloves with foreign merchants.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The author was a member of the Castilian fleet, so the account records the Europeans' side of the deal and not the Tidorese view.
design.evidence_quote: they settled to give for the bahar of cloves fourteen ells of yellow cloth

items.stem: After Akbar's forces conquered Bengal in 1576, the political integration described in the excerpt most likely involved which of the following Mughal administrative practices?

options.text: Appointing ranked mansabdars to govern provinces and collect land revenue for the emperor
options.label: key
options.why: Akbar organized imperial service through the mansabdar system. Ranked officials governed provinces such as Bengal and gathered land revenue for the center, which is how integration of a newly conquered province began.

options.text: Recruiting Christian boys through the devshirme to staff provincial governments and the elite janissary corps
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The devshirme was an Ottoman practice, not a Mughal one.

options.text: Selecting provincial officials through Confucian civil service examinations held in the imperial capital
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Civil service examinations were used in Ming and Qing China, not in the Mughal Empire.

options.text: Requiring Hindu landholders in conquered provinces to convert to Sunni Islam in order to keep their estates
options.label: reversal
options.why: Akbar was known for religious tolerance and for including non-Muslims in his government. He did not require landholders to convert.

facts: Akbar's forces conquered Bengal in 1576.
Akbar organized Mughal officials into the ranked mansabdar system in the late 1500s.
Akbar abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims in 1579 (some sources say 1564) and included Hindu Rajputs in his administration.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt says that political integration of Bengal began under the Mughals after Akbar's 1576 conquest, and the question asks how that integration was carried out.
design.evidence_quote: Under the Mughals, the political integration of Bengal with the rest of the subcontinent began

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the authors' explanation for why Bengal was never truly subjugated by the Mughal Empire?

options.text: Bengal's distance from Delhi and poor communications let local governors act independently
options.label: key
options.why: The authors explicitly blame remoteness and poor communications, which made it easy for local governors to ignore imperial directives.

options.text: Bengal's governors won independence by defeating Mughal armies in a series of open battles after 1576
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt mentions no battles after 1576. It describes governors quietly ignoring directives, not military victories.

options.text: The Mughal conquest fully absorbed Bengal into a centralized state whose officials closely obeyed imperial orders
options.label: reversal
options.why: This is the opposite of the excerpt's claim that Bengal was never truly subjugated.

options.text: Bengal's growing wealth from overseas textile trade with European merchants was the main source of its independence
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Bengal's textile trade was real, but the excerpt attributes the province's independence to geography and communications, not to trade wealth.

facts: Delhi was a principal Mughal capital, far to the northwest of Bengal.
Bengal was a Mughal province (subah) from the late 1500s into the 1700s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The final two sentences give remoteness from Delhi and poor lines of communication as the reasons governors could keep their independence.
design.evidence_quote: It was always too remote from the center of government in Delhi. Because lines of communications were poor

items.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most directly support the excerpt's argument that Bengal's local governors maintained their independence from the Mughal center?

options.text: In the early 1700s, Bengal's nawabs ran provincial revenue and appointments with little oversight from Delhi
options.label: key
options.why: Under Murshid Quli Khan and his successors in the early 1700s, the nawabs of Bengal ran the province with growing independence from Delhi. This directly supports the claim that governors ignored the imperial center.

options.text: Akbar's officials surveyed farmland across northern India and fixed tax rates collected for the imperial treasury in Delhi
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Akbar's revenue reforms show central power in the northern heartland. They say nothing about governors in Bengal acting on their own.

options.text: Aurangzeb led Mughal armies south in the 1680s and annexed the Deccan sultanates of Bijapur and Golconda to the empire
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This shows the empire expanding in the south. It does not support the claim about Bengali autonomy and, if anything, points to strong central power.

options.text: Portuguese merchants established trading posts along the Bengal coast in the 1500s to buy cotton cloth and rice
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: European trade in Bengal is real, but it has nothing to do with whether governors obeyed Delhi.

facts: Murshid Quli Khan governed Bengal in the early 1700s and became its first nawab around 1717, with growing autonomy from Delhi.
Aurangzeb annexed Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687).
The Portuguese set up trading posts in Bengal in the 1500s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt argues that local governors ignored imperial directives, so evidence of eighteenth-century nawabs governing with little oversight would support it.
design.evidence_quote: local governors found it easy to ignore imperial directives and maintain their independence

items.stem: The excerpt's reference to the beginning of Mughal decline in the eighteenth century is best understood in the context of which broader development?

options.text: The rise of regional powers such as the Marathas after the death of Aurangzeb in 1707
options.label: key
options.why: After Aurangzeb died in 1707, Maratha expansion and increasingly independent provincial governors broke Mughal central power. This is the decline the excerpt refers to.

options.text: The Indian Rebellion of 1857, after which the British exiled the last Mughal emperor and ended the dynasty
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The 1857 rebellion came long after the decline began. It marks the formal end of the dynasty, not the start of its eighteenth-century decline.

options.text: The Portuguese seizure of Goa in 1510, which gave a European power its first fortified base on the Indian coast
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The capture of Goa happened before the Mughal Empire was founded in 1526, so it cannot explain eighteenth-century decline.

options.text: The emergence of Sikhism in Punjab in the 1500s as a devotional faith that drew on Hindu and Muslim traditions
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The founding of Sikhism was a sixteenth-century religious development. It does not explain the political breakup of the 1700s.

facts: Aurangzeb died in 1707.
The Marathas expanded their power across much of India in the 1700s.
The British exiled the last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah II, after the 1857 rebellion.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt dates the end of Bengal's status as a Mughal province to the start of Mughal decline in the eighteenth century, and the question asks students to place that decline in context.
design.evidence_quote: Bengal remained a Mughal province until the beginning of the decline of the Mughal Empire in the eighteenth century

items.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of the excerpt for a historian studying Bengal under Mughal rule?

options.text: As a brief modern overview, it offers little detail on how people in Bengal experienced Mughal rule
options.label: key
options.why: The credit and context lines show it is a short summary in a late-1980s reference book. It gives broad political points but no detail on local experience.

options.text: As a record written by Mughal court historians, it likely exaggerates how firmly Delhi controlled distant provinces
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The source was written by Library of Congress researchers in the 1980s, not by Mughal court historians, and it stresses weak control rather than exaggerating it.

options.text: As a work produced centuries after the events, it has no value at all as evidence about Bengal under the Mughal Empire
options.label: overstated
options.why: Secondary sources written long after events can still be valuable. Saying it has no value at all goes too far.

options.text: As a study commissioned by the British East India Company, it reflects a goal of justifying the colonial annexation of Bengal
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The context line says it was written for the U.S. government in the late 1980s, not for the East India Company.

facts: The source is a 1989 Library of Congress country study written for the U.S. government.
The British East India Company gained control of Bengal after the Battle of Plassey in 1757.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line describes the work as a late-1980s reference book that summarizes Bengal's pre-British history.

items.stem: The relationship between Bengal's governors and the Mughal center described in the excerpt was most similar to which of the following developments in another land-based empire?

options.text: Ottoman provincial notables (ayans) gaining local power as central authority weakened in the 1700s
options.label: key
options.why: In the eighteenth century, Ottoman provincial notables collected taxes and kept their own forces with growing independence from Istanbul. This parallels Bengal's governors ignoring Delhi.

options.text: Tokugawa shoguns requiring daimyo to spend alternate years at Edo, keeping regional lords under close watch
options.label: reversal
options.why: Alternate attendance was a tool of strong central control over regional lords, the opposite of Bengal's autonomy.

options.text: Shah Abbas I using ghulam slave soldiers loyal to the throne to weaken the power of Safavid tribal chiefs
options.label: reversal
options.why: Abbas I's reforms centralized power and reduced provincial autonomy rather than showing it.

options.text: Peter the Great forcing Russian nobles into state service and ranking them in a new Table of Ranks in 1722
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Table of Ranks bound elites more tightly to the central state, which is not like Bengal's independent governors.

facts: Ottoman ayans gained significant regional power in the eighteenth century.
The Tokugawa shogunate made alternate attendance (sankin-kotai) a formal requirement in 1635.
Peter the Great introduced the Table of Ranks in 1722.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt describes provincial governors in a distant province acting independently of a weakening imperial center, which students compare with other empires.
design.evidence_quote: Bengal was never truly subjugated

items.stem: The "recent foreign acquisitions of Chinese territory" that Giles mentions are best explained as part of which of the following processes?

options.text: European powers and Japan seizing leaseholds and spheres of influence after China's 1895 defeat by Japan
options.label: key
options.why: After the Sino-Japanese War, the powers scrambled for concessions in 1897-1898. Germany's seizure of Jiaozhou Bay in Shandong (Shantung) fits Giles's link between new territorial losses and unrest in that province.

options.text: Britain's annexation of Hong Kong Island under the Treaty of Nanjing that ended the First Opium War in 1842
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Hong Kong Island was ceded in 1842, more than fifty years before the Boxer unrest, so it was not one of the recent acquisitions Giles describes.

options.text: Japan's creation of the puppet state of Manchukuo in northeastern China after its army seized Manchuria in 1931
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Manchukuo was created in 1932, decades after the events of 1899-1900 and after Giles published his book in 1912.

options.text: Western states replacing Qing governors with their own officials and ruling China's coastal provinces as formal colonies
options.label: overstated
options.why: The foreign powers held leaseholds, treaty ports and spheres of influence. China was never divided into formal colonies, and Qing officials still governed the provinces.

facts: Japan defeated China in the Sino-Japanese War of 1894-1895.
Germany seized Jiaozhou Bay in Shandong in 1897 and obtained a lease there in 1898, part of the scramble for concessions in which other powers also gained leaseholds.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Giles ties unrest in Shantung to 'recent foreign acquisitions of Chinese territory', which points to the leaseholds of 1897-1898.
design.evidence_quote: aggravated by recent foreign acquisitions of Chinese territory

items.stem: Giles's account of the events of 1900 most likely reflects which of the following points of view?

options.text: A British scholar's sympathy for foreign victims and readiness to blame the Qing court
options.label: key
options.why: Giles was a British professor. He stresses the suffering of besieged foreigners and murdered missionaries and blames the Manchus and the Empress Dowager for taking over the movement.

options.text: A Chinese nationalist's praise of the Boxers as patriots resisting Western and Japanese imperialism
options.label: reversal
options.why: Giles calls the movement a 'bloodthirsty anti-foreign outbreak', which is the opposite of praise. The credit line also identifies him as British.

options.text: A Qing official's effort to shield the Empress Dowager from foreign blame for the attacks on foreigners
options.label: reversal
options.why: Giles was a Cambridge professor, not a Qing official, and he accuses the Empress Dowager of complicity rather than defending her.

options.text: A socialist's view of the uprising as a class struggle of peasants against Chinese landlords
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt never discusses landlords or class conflict. It explains the movement through dynastic politics, hostility toward Christian converts and anti-foreign feeling.

facts: Herbert Giles was a British professor of Chinese at Cambridge who published China and the Manchus in 1912.
Boxers besieged the foreign legations in Beijing in the summer of 1900.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line identifies the author as a British Cambridge scholar, and the text dwells on foreign victims and blames the Empress Dowager.
design.evidence_quote: taken over by the Manchus, with the complicity of the Empress Dowager, as a means of getting rid of all the foreigners

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would most directly support Giles's claim that the Manchu court took over the Boxer movement?

options.text: The Qing court declared war on the foreign powers in June 1900 as Boxers besieged the legations
options.label: key
options.why: The court's declaration of war, issued while Boxers were attacking foreigners in Beijing, shows the dynasty adopting the movement's anti-foreign aims. This backs Giles's claim of court complicity.

options.text: Several governors in southern China ignored the court's orders and kept their provinces at peace with foreigners
options.label: reversal
options.why: This is accurate, but it shows that many Qing officials refused to join the anti-foreign campaign. It weakens Giles's claim rather than supporting it.

options.text: Boxer recruits practiced martial arts and rituals that they believed made them immune to foreign bullets
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This describes the Boxers' own beliefs and practices. It says nothing about whether the Manchu court took control of the movement.

options.text: Treaties signed in 1858 and 1860 gave Christian missionaries the right to preach in China's interior
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This helps explain the anger toward converts that Giles mentions, but it is not evidence that the court took over the movement.

facts: In June 1900 the Qing court under Empress Dowager Cixi declared war on the foreign powers.
Several governors in southern and central China refused to carry out the court's anti-foreign orders in 1900.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Giles's final sentence claims the Manchus and the Empress Dowager took over the movement, and the court's declaration of war is direct evidence for that claim.
design.evidence_quote: it was taken over by the Manchus, with the complicity of the Empress Dowager

items.stem: The events described in the excerpt most directly contributed to which of the following developments in the early 1900s?

options.text: A large indemnity under the 1901 Boxer Protocol that further weakened the Qing before its fall
options.label: key
options.why: After foreign troops relieved the legations, the 1901 Boxer Protocol forced China to pay a huge indemnity. This drained the treasury and discredited the dynasty, which fell in 1911-1912.

options.text: The withdrawal of foreign powers from their Chinese spheres of influence after the legations were relieved
options.label: reversal
options.why: The intervention increased foreign influence. The powers kept their spheres and won the right to station troops in Beijing.

options.text: The launch of the Self-Strengthening Movement, in which Qing officials built arsenals and modern shipyards
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Self-Strengthening Movement began in the 1860s, decades before the Boxer crisis, so it could not have been caused by it.

options.text: The Taiping Rebellion's attempt to replace Qing rule with a Heavenly Kingdom inspired by Christian teaching
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Taiping Rebellion took place from 1850 to 1864, long before the events of 1900.

facts: The Boxer Protocol of 1901 required China to pay a large indemnity to the foreign powers.
The Qing dynasty was overthrown in the revolution of 1911-1912.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt describes the 1900 siege of the legations and the anti-foreign violence that led to the foreign intervention and the Boxer Protocol.
design.evidence_quote: the siege of the Legations

items.stem: The "ill-feeling between the people at large and converts to Christianity" described in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which development?

options.text: Unequal treaties that let foreign missionaries work across China under foreign legal protection
options.label: key
options.why: Treaties forced on China after the Opium Wars opened the interior to missionaries and gave them, and often their converts, the backing of foreign powers. This caused resentment in places like Shandong.

options.text: Jesuit missionaries serving as astronomers and mapmakers at the Ming and early Qing courts in the 1600s
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Jesuits at court belong to the 1600s and early 1700s and worked mostly among the elite. They do not explain village tensions in the 1890s.

options.text: Spanish friars converting much of the Philippine population to Catholicism during centuries of colonial rule
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Catholic conversion in the Spanish Philippines happened in another region and has no direct link to conflict between Chinese villagers and converts.

options.text: Hong Xiuquan's claim to be Jesus's younger brother, which inspired the Taiping Rebellion against the Qing
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is accurate Chinese history, but the Taiping movement ended in 1864. It does not explain the tensions with converts under treaty protection that led to the Boxer movement.

facts: The Treaty of Tianjin (1858) and the Convention of Beijing (1860) allowed Christian missionaries to work in China's interior.
The Opium Wars (1839-1842 and 1856-1860) ended in treaties that gave foreign powers special privileges in China.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Giles traces the unrest in Shantung to hostility toward Christian converts, whose position rested on missionary rights won through the unequal treaties.
design.evidence_quote: ill-feeling between the people at large and converts to Christianity

items.stem: The anti-foreign rising Giles describes in China is most similar to which development in another region in the period 1750 to 1900?

options.text: The Indian Rebellion of 1857, in which sepoys and others rose against British East India Company rule
options.label: key
options.why: Like the Boxer movement, the 1857 rebellion was a violent rising against foreign power that was partly driven by fear of Christian influence on local religion, and foreign forces put it down.

options.text: The Meiji Restoration, in which Japanese reformers adopted Western industry, schooling, and a conscript army
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Meiji Restoration answered Western pressure by having the state adopt Western models, not by a popular rising to drive out foreigners.

options.text: Muhammad Ali's program in Egypt of building state-owned textile factories and a modern army in the early 1800s
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Muhammad Ali's program was a state-led modernization effort, not a popular anti-foreign uprising like the one Giles describes.

options.text: The Ottoman Tanzimat reforms, which reorganized law and administration along European lines in the mid-1800s
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Tanzimat were government reforms that borrowed European models. They were the opposite of an anti-foreign outbreak.

facts: The Indian Rebellion of 1857 was a large uprising against British East India Company rule, which British forces suppressed.
After the rebellion, the British Crown took direct control of India in 1858.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Giles calls the movement an 'anti-foreign outbreak' fed by resentment of Christian converts, which matches the anti-foreign and religious grievances behind the 1857 rebellion.
design.evidence_quote: became a bloodthirsty anti-foreign outbreak

items.stem: The scene in Zhang Zeduan's early 12th-century painting most directly reflects which historical situation in China?

options.text: A period of commercial expansion and urban growth in China
options.label: key
options.why: The crowded bridge, market stalls, carts and cargo boats show a busy commercial city. That matches the well-documented commercial and urban growth of the Song dynasty, which ruled from 960 to 1279.

options.text: The disruption of Chinese cities following the Mongol conquest of the Southern Song
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Mongols completed their conquest of the Song in 1279, more than a century after this early 12th-century painting.

options.text: The isolation of Chinese ports after Ming rulers ended the voyages of Zheng He
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Zheng He's voyages ended in the 1430s, long after the Song painting was made.

options.text: A decline of markets as Confucian officials banned private trade in cities
options.label: reversal
options.why: Private urban trade grew under the Song, and the painting shows thriving markets, not a decline.

facts: The Song dynasty ruled China from 960 to 1279.
Song China saw major growth in commerce and in the size of its cities.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The market stalls, the crowds and the loaded boats around the bridge show commercial bustle, and the credit line dates the painting to the Song dynasty in the early 12th century.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main idea the painting conveys about the city it depicts?

options.text: City life depended on trade moved by both river boats and road traffic
options.label: key
options.why: The detail sets cargo boats on the river beside carts, pack animals and porters on the bridge and the street. Together they show water and land transport feeding the city's commerce.

options.text: City life centered on state ceremonies led by Confucian scholar-officials
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The image shows ordinary traders and laborers at work, not official ceremonies.

options.text: The city was preparing its walls and troops to resist a nomadic invasion
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: No soldiers or fortifications appear in the detail. The scene is commercial and peaceful.

options.text: City streets were reserved mainly for Buddhist monks traveling to monastery shrines
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The figures are porters, vendors and travelers with goods, not a religious procession.

facts: Song cities relied on river and canal transport as well as overland traffic to bring in goods.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Loaded cargo boats on the river appear alongside carts, pack animals and crowds of porters on the bridge and at the market stalls.

items.stem: The cargo boats on the river in the painting are best understood in the context of which broader development in Song China?

options.text: Growing internal trade on canals and rivers linking regions of China
options.label: key
options.why: Song China's economy depended on waterways such as the Grand Canal, which carried grain and goods between south and north. The river traffic in the painting fits this pattern.

options.text: Imperial treasure fleets dominating Indian Ocean trade under Admiral Zheng He
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Zheng He's fleets sailed from 1405 to 1433 under the Ming, not during the Song.

options.text: Caravan trade on the Silk Roads expanding under the protection of the Pax Mongolica
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Pax Mongolica belongs to the 13th and 14th centuries. It also involved overland caravans, not river boats.

options.text: State limits on private trade that confined sales to official walled markets
options.label: reversal
options.why: The strict official market system of the Tang broke down under the Song, and commerce spread into the streets, as the painting shows.

facts: The Grand Canal, completed under the Sui dynasty in the early 7th century, linked northern and southern China.
Under the Song, internal trade along canals and rivers expanded greatly.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Several cargo boats crowd the river beneath and beside the bridge, which shows that the city's commerce relied on water transport.

items.stem: The commercial activity shown in the painting is most similar to which development in another region between c. 1200 and c. 1450?

options.text: The growth of trading cities such as Venice and Genoa in the Mediterranean
options.label: key
options.why: Like Song cities, Italian city-states grew into crowded commercial centers built on water-borne trade during this period.

options.text: The spread of manorialism, which tied European peasants to largely self-sufficient estates
options.label: reversal
options.why: Manorialism was a rural, largely self-sufficient system. It is the opposite of the urban market economy shown in the painting.

options.text: The Inca use of mit'a labor to build roads serving state needs rather than private markets
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Inca did use mit'a labor for roads, but that served state redistribution, not private commerce like the markets in the painting.

options.text: The rise of Mughal Delhi as a commercial hub after Babur's conquest of northern India
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Babur founded the Mughal Empire in 1526, after the c. 1200 to c. 1450 period.

facts: Venice and Genoa became major Mediterranean trading powers in the 13th and 14th centuries.
Babur founded the Mughal Empire in 1526.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The painting's busy markets, boats and bridge traffic show a dense commercial city, which students can compare to other trading cities of the period.

items.stem: Which of the following most directly helped Song China feed the large urban populations suggested by the crowded street in the painting?

options.text: Fast-ripening Champa rice that raised harvests in southern China
options.label: key
options.why: Champa rice, brought from Southeast Asia in the early 11th century, allowed more than one harvest a year. The extra food supported population growth and large cities under the Song.

options.text: Maize and sweet potatoes introduced from the Americas by Iberian traders
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: American crops reached China through the Columbian Exchange in the 16th century, long after the Song.

options.text: Grain sent as tribute from Central Asian oases under Mongol imperial rule
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Song China fed itself mainly from its own rice-growing south, not with Central Asian grain, and Mongol rule came later.

options.text: Enclosure of common lands that pushed displaced peasants into the cities
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Enclosure was a British development of later centuries, not a cause of Song urban growth.

facts: Champa rice was introduced into Song China from Southeast Asia in the early 11th century.
Song China's population grew substantially during the dynasty.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The dense crowds on the bridge and in the street suggest a large urban population that needed a steady food supply.

items.stem: A historian using the painting as evidence of living conditions across all of Song China would be most limited by which feature of the source?

options.text: It shows one city scene, though most Song subjects were rural farmers
options.label: key
options.why: The detail shows a single bustling urban setting. Most of the Song population lived and farmed in the countryside, so the painting cannot represent conditions everywhere.

options.text: It was made by a foreign envoy unfamiliar with Chinese customs and dress
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The credit line names Zhang Zeduan, a Song dynasty painter, not a foreign visitor.

options.text: It was painted long after the Song, during the Qing dynasty's last decades
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The original scroll is dated to the early 12th century, during the Song itself.

options.text: It portrays only elite scholar-officials at leisure and omits merchants and laborers
options.label: reversal
options.why: The image is full of porters, vendors, boatmen and carters, so it does not leave out working people.

facts: Most people in Song China lived in rural areas and worked in agriculture, even as cities grew.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The detail shows only a crowded urban bridge and market, and the context line says it depicts a Chinese city.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains Jahangir's purpose in describing the Chain of Justice in his memoirs?

options.text: To present himself as a just ruler who shielded subjects from abusive officials
options.label: key
options.why: Jahangir says the chain let 'the oppressed' get his attention if officials delayed justice or acted with hypocrisy. Recording it as his first order presents the new emperor as personally guarding justice, which supported the legitimacy of his reign.

options.text: To announce that Mughal law would henceforth follow strict Sharia rules over the Hindu majority
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the excerpt imposes strict religious law. The inheritance order applies to 'unbeliever or Musalman' alike.

options.text: To invite European trading companies to settle at Agra under the emperor's direct protection
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt never mentions Europeans. The chain is aimed at the emperor's own oppressed subjects.

options.text: To explain new rules for promoting officials through the ranks of the mansabdari system
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The mansabdari ranking system was real, but the chain concerns petitions for justice, not the promotion of officials.

facts: Jahangir ruled the Mughal Empire from 1605 to 1627.
Agra was a principal Mughal capital and fortress in the early 1600s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The chain is described as a way for the oppressed to reach the emperor when officials delayed or practised hypocrisy.
design.evidence_quote: the oppressed might come to this chain and shake it so that its noise might attract attention

items.stem: Which of the following claims does Jahangir make about the jagirdars in the excerpt?

options.text: Some had imposed tolls and cesses on their own authority for private profit
options.label: key
options.why: The first rule forbids the tamgha, the river tolls and 'other burdens' that the jagirdars had imposed 'for their own profit.'

options.text: They had been robbing merchant caravans themselves along remote imperial roads
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt mentions robberies on roads, but it tells jagirdars to build rest-houses there. It does not accuse them of the robberies.

options.text: Their land assignments should be abolished and placed entirely under khalisa management
options.label: overstated
options.why: The excerpt mentions khalisa lands only for roads that lie near them. It does not abolish jagirs.

options.text: They had failed to collect the tamgha and river tolls owed to the imperial treasury
options.label: reversal
options.why: Jahangir bans these levies. He does not complain that they went uncollected.

facts: Jagirdars were Mughal officials assigned the revenue of specific lands (jagirs).
Khalisa lands were revenue lands managed directly by the Mughal state.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Order (1) bans cesses that jagirdars had imposed for their own profit.
design.evidence_quote: other burdens which the jagirdars of every province and district had imposed for their own profit

items.stem: Jahangir's orders protecting merchants' bales and building rest-houses along roads are best understood in the context of which development in the period c. 1450 to c. 1750?

options.text: Mughal India's large export trade in textiles, which drew in silver
options.label: key
options.why: Mughal India was a major producer and exporter of cotton textiles, and silver flowed in to pay for them. Safe roads, sara'is and limits on interference with merchants supported this commerce.

options.text: The collapse of overland trade across Eurasia after the end of the Mongol khanates
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Mongol khanates broke apart in the 1300s, well before this period, and overland trade went on in Mughal India. The orders assume an active trade.

options.text: The British East India Company's takeover of tax collection in Bengal after Plassey
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Plassey (1757) and the Company's revenue rights in Bengal (1765) came long after Jahangir's reign.

options.text: The Ming dynasty's ban on private maritime trade to limit contact with foreigners
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Ming maritime trade ban was a Chinese policy and does not explain Mughal road and merchant regulations.

facts: Mughal India exported large quantities of cotton textiles in the 1600s and received silver in payment.
The Battle of Plassey took place in 1757.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Orders (2) and (3) protect travel and merchants' goods on roads.
design.evidence_quote: The bales of merchants should not be opened on the roads without informing them and obtaining their leave.

items.stem: Jahangir's order that the property of any subject, 'whether unbeliever or Musalman,' pass to his heirs is most consistent with which earlier Mughal development?

options.text: Akbar's policies accommodating non-Muslims, such as abolishing the jizya
options.label: key
options.why: Jahangir's father Akbar ended the jizya (1579) and courted Hindu elites. Applying the inheritance rule to Muslims and non-Muslims alike continues that accommodating approach.

options.text: Aurangzeb's reimposition of the jizya tax on non-Muslim subjects in 1679
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Aurangzeb's reimposition came after Jahangir's reign, not before, and it reversed accommodation rather than continuing it.

options.text: Babur's founding of the dynasty after defeating the Delhi Sultanate at Panipat in 1526
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Babur did found the dynasty at Panipat, but that conquest has nothing to do with equal inheritance rights for Muslims and non-Muslims.

options.text: The adoption of the Ottoman devshirme system to recruit non-Muslim boys for state service
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The devshirme was an Ottoman practice, not a Mughal one.

facts: Akbar (ruled 1556-1605) ended the jizya on non-Muslims, by most accounts in 1579.
Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya in 1679.
Babur defeated the Delhi Sultanate at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Order (4) protects inheritances for both non-Muslims and Muslims without distinction.
design.evidence_quote: if anyone, whether unbeliever or Musalman, should die, his property and effects should be left for his heirs

items.stem: The jagirdars named in the excerpt were part of which Mughal method of governing the empire's provinces?

options.text: Granting ranked officials land revenue in return for military service
options.label: key
options.why: Under the mansabdari system, ranked officials received jagirs, which were assignments of land revenue, in exchange for military and administrative service. That is why jagirdars could levy dues in their districts.

options.text: Selecting provincial officials through Confucian-style civil service examinations
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Civil service examinations belong to imperial China, not the Mughal Empire.

options.text: Allowing hereditary nobles to own land outright as private, untaxed estates
options.label: reversal
options.why: Jagirs were revenue assignments, usually not hereditary and often transferred. Jahangir can also give jagirdars orders in this excerpt.

options.text: Leasing provincial tax collection to European chartered trading companies
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: European companies won revenue rights in India only in the later 1700s, after this period.

facts: Under Akbar, Mughal officials (mansabdars) held numbered ranks and were often paid through jagirs, assignments of land revenue.
Jagirs were generally not hereditary and were periodically reassigned.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt refers to jagirdars of every province and district who imposed levies and could be ordered to build sara'is.
design.evidence_quote: the jagirdars of the neighbourhood should build sara'is (public rest-houses), mosques, and dig wells

items.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of the excerpt for historians studying how the Mughal Empire was actually governed under Jahangir?

options.text: It records the emperor's orders but not whether officials enforced them
options.label: key
options.why: Jahangir wrote the memoir himself and lists what he commanded. It cannot show how far jagirdars and other officials obeyed, so other evidence is needed.

options.text: It was written by a European visitor unfamiliar with Mughal court and provincial practice
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The credit line names the author as Jahangir himself, not a European visitor.

options.text: It describes only the reign of Akbar, before Jahangir took the throne
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The context says Jahangir describes his own orders from the start of his reign in 1605.

options.text: It covers religious matters only and says nothing about trade or taxation
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt directly addresses tolls, merchants' bales and roads.

facts: Jahangir wrote his memoirs, the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, during his reign (1605-1627).

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line and context show this is the emperor's own account of the orders he issued, so it records his intentions.
design.evidence_quote: I also gave twelve orders to be observed as rules of conduct (dasturu-l-`amal) in all my dominions

items.stem: The concern described in the excerpt about "the proper relation of Singaporeans to worldwide popular culture" is best explained by which development of the late twentieth century?

options.text: The worldwide spread of mass media and consumer entertainment, much of it from the United States
options.label: key
options.why: Starting after 1945, film, television, music, and consumer brands, many of them American, spread worldwide. That spread made the "worldwide popular culture" the passage mentions a live issue for Singapore's leaders.

options.text: The export of Soviet socialist realist art and film to newly independent states across Southeast Asia during the Cold War
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Soviet cultural exports were real, but they were not the popular culture Singapore's leaders worried about. The passage sets Asian roots against Western influence, not Soviet influence.

options.text: The circulation of Maoist revolutionary posters and slogans promoted abroad by China during the Cultural Revolution years
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Maoist propaganda was political material from Asia. It was not the global Western popular culture the passage describes.

options.text: The expansion of Christian missionary schooling under British colonial rule in the Straits Settlements
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Missionary schooling belongs to the colonial period before 1965. It does not explain the debates about worldwide popular culture in the late 1980s and 1990s.

facts: After 1945, American films, television, and music spread widely around the world.
Singapore became an independent country in 1965.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The passage says there was public discussion of how Singaporeans should relate to worldwide popular culture.
design.evidence_quote: the proper relation of Singaporeans to worldwide popular culture

items.stem: According to the excerpt, public discussion of identity in Singapore around 1990 tended to do which of the following?

options.text: Sort behavior into separate Asian and Western categories, often at leaders' prompting
options.label: key
options.why: The passage says these discussions were often started by political leaders and tended to split habits into separate "Asian" or "Western" categories.

options.text: Reject modernization entirely in favor of restoring precolonial village customs and economies
options.label: overstated
options.why: The passage says Singapore should be "modernized" but not Westernized, so leaders did not reject modernization.

options.text: Encourage Singaporeans to become fully Westernized in order to compete in the global economy
options.label: reversal
options.why: The passage says it would be a mistake for Singaporeans to become so Westernized that they lost touch with their Asian roots.

options.text: Originate mainly among opposition groups protesting the government's discriminatory ethnic policies
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The passage says political leaders often started these discussions, and it calls Singapore's stated values nondiscriminatory.

facts: Lee Kuan Yew served as Singapore's prime minister from 1959 to 1990.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The passage says the discussion was often started by political leaders and divided behavior into Asian or Western categories.
design.evidence_quote: tended to dichotomize habits and behavior into mutually exclusive "Asian" or "Western" categories

items.stem: Which historical situation most directly helps explain why Singapore's leaders after 1965 were preoccupied with defining a distinctive "Singaporean identity"?

options.text: Singapore was a new state whose population mixed Chinese, Malay, and Indian communities
options.label: key
options.why: Singapore became independent in 1965 after leaving Malaysia, and its population was made up of several ethnic communities. Leaders wanted a shared national identity that would sit above those ethnic loyalties.

options.text: Singapore had been occupied by Japanese forces during the Second World War until Japan's surrender in 1945
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Japanese occupation did happen, but it ended two decades before independence. It does not explain the later debates over Asian and Western values.

options.text: Singapore joined Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and the Philippines in founding ASEAN as a regional bloc in 1967
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Singapore did help found ASEAN in 1967. However, regional diplomatic cooperation does not explain why leaders were focused on national identity inside the country.

options.text: Singapore's leaders were responding to the collapse of the Soviet Union and the end of the Cold War in 1991
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The research for the book was finished in 1989, and the concern with identity began long before the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.

facts: Singapore separated from Malaysia and became independent in 1965.
Singapore's population is mainly made up of Chinese, Malay, and Indian communities.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line gives the 1965 independence date, and the passage mentions ethnicity and the leadership's concern with a Singaporean identity.
design.evidence_quote: The content of the distinctive "Singaporean identity"

items.stem: EXTRA. The excerpt's premise that Singapore should be "modernized but not a Westernized society" most closely resembles which earlier approach to modernization?

options.text: Meiji Japan's adoption of Western industry while promoting loyalty to the emperor
options.label: key
options.why: Meiji Japan, starting in 1868, adopted Western technology and institutions while promoting loyalty to the emperor and Japanese traditions. This matches the idea of modernizing without giving up Asian values.

options.text: Mustafa Kemal Ataturk's Turkish reforms requiring Western dress, the Latin alphabet, and secular law codes
options.label: reversal
options.why: Ataturk's reforms of the 1920s openly treated Westernization as the route to modernity, which is the opposite of what the passage describes.

options.text: Mohandas Gandhi's call for Indians to spin homemade cloth and reject machine-made British textiles
options.label: reversal
options.why: Gandhi's swadeshi campaign was suspicious of industrial modernization itself. Singapore's leaders wanted to modernize.

options.text: Mao Zedong's Cultural Revolution campaign to destroy old customs, old ideas, old culture, and old habits
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Cultural Revolution, starting in 1966, attacked traditional culture. Singapore's leaders wanted to keep Asian roots and values.

facts: The Meiji Restoration began in Japan in 1868.
Ataturk's reforms in the 1920s and 1930s adopted the Latin alphabet and Western-style legal codes.
The Cultural Revolution in China began in 1966.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The passage says Singapore should be modernized but not Westernized, and should keep its Asian roots and values.
design.evidence_quote: Singapore should be a modernized but not a Westernized society

items.stem: EXTRA. Given that the excerpt comes from a reference book prepared by the Library of Congress for the United States government, which of the following is a likely limitation of the source?

options.text: It views official debates from outside and may not show how ordinary Singaporeans saw them
options.label: key
options.why: The authors were outside observers who mostly describe debates started by leaders. The source may therefore say little about how ordinary Singaporeans felt about cosmopolitan and traditional values.

options.text: It was written by Singapore's ruling party, so it mainly repeats government propaganda about Asian values
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The credit line shows the book was written by the U.S. Library of Congress, not by any Singaporean political party.

options.text: It was completed before Singapore became independent, so it cannot address questions of national identity
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The research was finished in 1989, long after Singapore became independent in 1965.

options.text: It was designed to persuade Singaporeans to adopt American culture, so it exaggerates Western influence
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the credit line or the text suggests the book was meant to persuade Singaporeans. It is a reference work written for the U.S. government.

facts: Singapore became independent in 1965.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says the book was written for the U.S. government around 1990, and the text says the discussion was often started by political leaders.
design.evidence_quote: often initiated by political leaders

items.stem: The plan described in the excerpt to build "a very powerful steam fleet" best illustrates which of the following processes in the nineteenth century?

options.text: Industrial advances in steam and iron gave Europeans new military tools for expanding control in Asia
options.label: key
options.why: The excerpt describes armed iron steamers built to add to the resources of the Company's Indian government and tested in China. Industrial technology of this kind gave European states a military edge that supported imperial expansion.

options.text: Qing officials adopted Western steamships and arsenals to strengthen the Chinese state against foreign pressure in the 1860s
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Self-Strengthening Movement was a Chinese response that came decades later. The excerpt describes British East India Company plans, not Qing ones.

options.text: British naval patrols used new steam vessels mainly to suppress the Atlantic slave trade off the coast of West Africa
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: British anti-slave-trade patrols did take place, but the excerpt is about Company steamers meant for China and India, not West Africa.

options.text: Industrial demand for raw cotton led British firms to replace Indian textile exports with cotton grown in Egypt
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Demand for raw materials was a real feature of the period, but the excerpt is about military steam technology, not cotton supply.

facts: The Nemesis, an iron steamer, was built in 1839 for the East India Company.
Steam-powered gunboats such as the Nemesis were used by Britain in the First Opium War (1839-1842).

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt describes armed iron steamers intended to become a steam fleet serving the Company's Indian government.
design.evidence_quote: by degrees a very powerful steam fleet would become an invaluable addition to the already vast resources of the Indian government

items.stem: Hall's description of China's coastal rivers as "an admirable field for these experiments" most likely reflects which point of view?

options.text: A British officer viewing the war in China as a chance to test tools for extending Company power
options.label: key
options.why: Hall commanded the Nemesis in the First Opium War. He treats China's rivers as a testing ground whose results could be applied to the Company's territories, which reflects a British imperial point of view.

options.text: A Qing official alarmed that armed foreign steamers could move far up rivers and threaten inland Chinese cities
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The author was a British naval officer, not a Chinese official. The excerpt presents the steamers' river capability as an advantage, not a threat.

options.text: A critic of the opium trade who argued that the war was damaging Britain's moral standing in Asia
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt says nothing critical about opium or the war. It speaks approvingly of the steamers' potential.

options.text: A merchant mainly concerned with surveying China's rivers to expand legitimate tea exports to Britain
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The rivers are mentioned as a place to test armed vessels, not as trade routes. The author was a naval commander, not a merchant.

facts: William Hall commanded the Nemesis during the First Opium War (1839-1842).

design.key_evidence_in_source: The author, a British commander, frames China's unsurveyed rivers as a place to test steamers whose success would benefit the Company's territories.
design.evidence_quote: presented an admirable field for these experiments

items.stem: Sending armed iron steamers to China around 1840, as described in the excerpt, is best understood in the context of which broader development?

options.text: British efforts to force the Qing to open trade, especially to opium grown in India
options.label: key
options.why: The Nemesis was sent to China for the First Opium War. Britain fought that war to protect the opium trade from British India and to force wider access to Chinese markets.

options.text: The Taiping Rebellion, a massive uprising that challenged Qing rule across southern and central China
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Taiping Rebellion began in 1850, after the voyages of 1840 to 1843 described in the source.

options.text: Meiji reforms in Japan that created a modern navy modeled closely on the British Royal Navy
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Meiji Restoration began in 1868, decades after the Nemesis was built. It also concerns Japan, not British action in China.

options.text: Russian expansion across Central Asia that alarmed British officials responsible for India
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Rivalry with Russia in Central Asia was real, but it does not explain why Britain sent river steamers to fight in China.

facts: Britain fought the First Opium War (1839-1842) after the Qing tried to suppress the opium trade.
Much of the opium sold in China was grown in British-controlled India.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says the Nemesis was sent to China and served in the First Opium War, and the excerpt links China operations to the Company's Indian government.
design.evidence_quote: the numerous rivers along the coast of China, hitherto very imperfectly known, and almost totally unsurveyed

items.stem: The use of armed steamers described in the excerpt is most similar to which later nineteenth-century development?

options.text: The US use of steam warships to pressure Japan into opening its ports in the 1850s
options.label: key
options.why: Commodore Perry's steam-powered squadron (1853-1854) also used industrial naval technology to force an Asian state to open to trade, which parallels the steamers' role in China.

options.text: The Sepoy Rebellion of 1857, in which Indian soldiers rose against East India Company rule
options.label: reversal
options.why: This was resistance against Company power, not a use of technology to extend it.

options.text: The Meiji government's abolition of samurai privileges in order to build a national conscript army
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This was an internal Japanese military reform, not an industrial power using steam technology to coerce another state.

options.text: The Ottoman Tanzimat reforms, which reorganized law and administration along European lines
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Tanzimat was a defensive reform program inside the Ottoman Empire. It has nothing to do with naval coercion abroad.

facts: Commodore Matthew Perry led US steam warships to Japan in 1853-1854, leading to the Treaty of Kanagawa (1854).

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt describes armed, well-funded steamers sent to operate against an Asian state's coasts and rivers.
design.evidence_quote: They were all to be adequately armed and manned

items.stem: British use of steamers such as the Nemesis in the war described in the context line contributed most directly to which outcome?

options.text: The Treaty of Nanjing, which ceded Hong Kong to Britain and opened ports to trade
options.label: key
options.why: British naval superiority, including steamers like the Nemesis, helped win the First Opium War. The war ended with the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842, which ceded Hong Kong and opened five treaty ports.

options.text: The end of the East India Company's long-held monopoly over all British trade with China
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Company's China trade monopoly ended in 1833, before the Nemesis was built, so the war could not have caused it.

options.text: The Boxer Rebellion's attacks on foreigners and Chinese Christians in northern China
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Boxer Rebellion took place around 1899 to 1901, too far removed from the war to be its most direct outcome.

options.text: The Qing decision to ban opium imports and to seize and destroy British opium stocks at Canton
options.label: reversal
options.why: Lin Zexu's seizure of opium in 1839 was a cause of the war, not a result of British steam power.

facts: The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) ended the First Opium War, ceded Hong Kong to Britain and opened five treaty ports.
Lin Zexu destroyed confiscated opium at Canton in 1839.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line states that the Nemesis served in the First Opium War, whose outcome students must connect to the treaty settlement.

items.stem: Which of the following claims about iron steamers does the excerpt make?

options.text: Success in China would show their usefulness on rivers in Company-ruled India
options.label: key
options.why: The excerpt argues that success in China would show their value on the rivers of Hindostan and other Company territories.

options.text: They had already proven reliable in several earlier voyages around the Cape of Good Hope
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt states that no iron steamer had yet rounded the Cape, so their seaworthiness there was untested.

options.text: Their high cost made them impractical for most colonial governments in South Asia
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt says no reasonable expense was to be spared and calls a steam fleet invaluable to the Indian government.

options.text: They were designed mainly for open-ocean battles against rival European navies
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt says they were built with particular reference to river navigation, and it mentions no European rivals.

facts: The East India Company governed large territories in India in the 1840s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The author infers that success in China's rivers would prove the steamers' utility in India.
design.evidence_quote: their utility in the fine rivers and along the shores of Hindostan, and other portions of the Company's territories, would be demonstrated

items.stem: Which of the following best explains why so many colons left Algeria in 1962, as described in the excerpt?

options.text: Settlers expected to lose their privileged position once rule passed to the Muslim majority after a bitter war.
options.label: key
options.why: The excerpt says Europeans would have to become Algerian citizens or be treated as aliens with fewer rights. After more than a century of settler dominance and eight years of war, most colons would not live as a minority in an FLN-led state.

options.text: The Evian Accords required the French government to deport all European residents from Algeria within three years.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The accords did the opposite. They guaranteed colons property, civil and political rights for three years and then let them choose Algerian citizenship.

options.text: A League of Nations plan required population exchanges between new states, as Greece and Turkey had done in 1923.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Greek-Turkish exchange belongs to the interwar period, and the League of Nations no longer existed in 1962. No exchange plan applied to Algeria.

options.text: Postwar economic growth in France drew workers from across the Mediterranean into factories in Paris, Lyon and other cities.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: France's postwar boom did attract labor migrants, but it does not explain a sudden flight of settlers timed to the cease-fire and independence.

facts: French colonization of Algeria began in 1830.
The Algerian War of Independence lasted from 1954 to 1962.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt says that after three years Europeans had to become Algerian citizens or become aliens, and it describes the exodus that followed.
design.evidence_quote: Europeans would be obliged to become Algerian citizens or be classified as aliens with the attendant loss of rights

items.stem: According to the excerpt, which of the following best describes the outcome of the OAS campaign of 1962?

options.text: It caused the worst violence of the war but did not break the cease-fire or stop independence.
options.label: key
options.why: The author calls the campaign the worst carnage of the eight-year war but says it failed in its objectives. The OAS made a truce with the FLN in June, and independence followed in July.

options.text: It provoked the FLN into abandoning the cease-fire, which delayed Algerian independence until the late 1960s.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author says the OAS tried to provoke a break in the cease-fire and failed. Independence was declared on July 3, 1962.

options.text: It targeted Muslim civilians only, avoiding attacks on the French army and police that were enforcing the accords.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt says the terror was also aimed at the French army and police enforcing the accords.

options.text: It was secretly directed by de Gaulle's government to pressure the FLN into granting settlers permanent rights.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The OAS was a settler and dissident military group that opposed de Gaulle's policy and attacked French forces. It was not an instrument of the French government.

facts: The OAS was formed in 1961 by settlers and dissident French army officers who opposed Algerian independence.
Algeria became independent in July 1962.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The author judges that the OAS terror failed and notes the OAS-FLN truce of June 17, 1962.
design.evidence_quote: Ultimately, the terrorism failed in its objectives, and the OAS and the FLN concluded a truce on June 17, 1962.

items.stem: The end of French rule in Algeria described in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which broader development?

options.text: Weakened European powers' retreat from empire as nationalist movements grew after the Second World War
options.label: key
options.why: France came out of the Second World War weakened and lost Indochina in 1954. Around 1960 it gave up most of its African colonies, and the Algerian settlement was part of this wider European retreat from empire.

options.text: A Cold War agreement in which the United States and Soviet Union divided former colonies into spheres of influence
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: No superpower agreement divided the former colonies. The excerpt describes a settlement between France and the FLN.

options.text: The partition of Africa among European powers that had been arranged at the Berlin Conference in the 1880s
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Berlin Conference of 1884-1885 was about creating empires in Africa, not ending them.

options.text: Pan-Arab efforts to unite Arab states, such as the 1958 union of Egypt and Syria in the United Arab Republic
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The United Arab Republic was a real pan-Arab project, but Algeria never joined it, and it does not explain France's withdrawal.

facts: France was defeated at Dien Bien Phu in Indochina in 1954.
In 1960, many French colonies in sub-Saharan Africa became independent.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt describes a European power negotiating its withdrawal from a colony after a long war with a nationalist movement.
design.evidence_quote: Talks with the FLN reopened at Evian in May 1961

items.stem: The end of French rule in Algeria described in the excerpt was most similar to the end of British rule in which of the following places?

options.text: Kenya, where a settler minority and an armed revolt made the path to independence violent
options.label: key
options.why: Like Algeria, Kenya had a politically powerful European settler population and an armed anticolonial uprising, the Mau Mau revolt of the 1950s. Kenya became independent in 1963.

options.text: Ghana, where Nkrumah's party won elections and gained independence through a largely peaceful transfer in 1957
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is accurate about Ghana, but it is a contrast with Algeria. Ghana had no large settler community and no war of independence.

options.text: Hong Kong, which Britain returned to China in 1997 under an agreement negotiated with the government in Beijing
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The handover was a transfer between two states and did not follow an anticolonial war or settler violence. It is not comparable to Algeria.

options.text: Canada, which gained full self-government gradually through dominion status and the 1931 Statute of Westminster
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Canada's gradual, peaceful constitutional path belongs to an earlier era and differs sharply from Algeria's war.

facts: The Mau Mau uprising against British rule in Kenya took place in the 1950s.
Kenya became independent in 1963.
Ghana became independent under Kwame Nkrumah in 1957.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt stresses a large settler population (colons) and extreme violence during the shift to independence, which is what Algeria shares with Kenya.
design.evidence_quote: It was the most wanton carnage that Algeria had witnessed in eight years of savage warfare.

items.stem: Based on the context line and the passage, the author most likely wrote this passage in order to

options.text: give U.S. officials background on how Algeria won independence from France
options.label: key
options.why: The context line says the reference book was written for the U.S. government in the early 1990s. The passage gives a factual, chronological account of how the war ended.

options.text: persuade French voters to approve the Evian Accords in the June 1962 referendum
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The text was written about thirty years after the 1962 referendum, for the U.S. government rather than French voters.

options.text: defend the OAS campaign as a justified response to the loss of settler property rights
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author condemns the OAS campaign as wanton carnage and says it failed.

options.text: urge Washington to send military aid to the FLN during its war against the French army
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The war ended in 1962, long before this early-1990s reference work, and the passage does not argue for any policy.

facts: The Evian Accords were signed in March 1962 and approved by French voters in a referendum in 1962.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says the book was a reference work written for the U.S. government in the early 1990s.

items.stem: The July 1, 1962, referendum described in the excerpt best reflects which principle invoked by many anticolonial movements?

options.text: Self-determination, the right of a people to choose its own government
options.label: key
options.why: Algerian voters chose independence in a near-unanimous vote, which applies the principle of self-determination. That principle appears in the UN Charter and was central to anticolonial demands.

options.text: Non-alignment, the refusal of new states to join either the U.S. or Soviet bloc
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Independent Algeria did join the Non-Aligned Movement, but a vote on independence is about self-rule, not Cold War neutrality.

options.text: Negritude, a literary movement celebrating African identity against French cultural rule
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Negritude was a francophone Black literary and cultural movement. It was not the principle behind a vote on statehood.

options.text: Collective security, the pledge of League members to defend any member under attack
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Collective security concerned how states defend one another. It has nothing to do with a colony voting on independence.

facts: The UN Charter (1945) refers to the principle of self-determination of peoples.
Algeria became independent in July 1962 after a referendum.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt reports that nearly all of the Algerian electorate voted in the independence referendum and that the vote was nearly unanimous.
design.evidence_quote: some 6 million of a total Algerian electorate of 6.5 million cast their ballots in the referendum on independence
