items.stem: The privatization program described in the excerpt best illustrates which of the following developments?

options.text: The shift from state-directed economies toward market economies after the Cold War
options.label: key
options.why: The passage describes state enterprises in post-Soviet Russia passing into private hands, which is part of the move from a Soviet command economy to a market economy after 1991.

options.text: The expansion of state ownership of industry under Soviet Five-Year Plans in the 1930s
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Stalin's Five-Year Plans increased state control. They belong to an earlier period and run opposite to the privatization described.

options.text: The adoption of import substitution policies to protect national industries in Latin America
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Import substitution was a mid-century Latin American strategy that relied on state protection. It has nothing to do with selling off Russian state firms.

options.text: The nationalization of foreign-owned enterprises by newly independent states after decolonization
options.label: reversal
options.why: Nationalization moves ownership to the state, which is the reverse of the transfer to private owners in the excerpt.

facts: The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.
Russia began mass voucher privatization in 1992 under President Boris Yeltsin.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt reports that most Russian enterprises were transferred from the state to private owners after the Soviet collapse.
design.evidence_quote: transferring ownership of 70 percent of Russia's large and medium-sized enterprises to private hands

items.stem: Which of the following claims does the excerpt make about Russian privatization by the middle of 1994?

options.text: Most large and medium-sized state enterprises had been moved into private ownership
options.label: key
options.why: The excerpt states that 70 percent of large and medium-sized enterprises had been transferred to private hands by June 1994.

options.text: Most vouchers issued in 1992 remained unused because citizens distrusted the new firms
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt says 96 percent of the vouchers had already been used, sold or invested.

options.text: The State Duma enthusiastically endorsed cash sales of shares in remaining state firms
options.label: reversal
options.why: According to the excerpt, the Duma put up stiff opposition, and Yeltsin then used a decree.

options.text: Privatization concentrated ownership in the hands of a few wealthy financiers known as oligarchs
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Historians do discuss the rise of oligarchs in 1990s Russia, but this excerpt never mentions them or makes that claim.

facts: Russian vouchers were distributed to citizens beginning in 1992.
The State Duma became Russia's lower house of parliament under the 1993 constitution.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The opening sentences give the 70 percent figure for large and medium-sized enterprises as the program's achievement.
design.evidence_quote: It succeeded in transferring ownership of 70 percent of Russia's large and medium-sized enterprises to private hands

items.stem: The privatization described in the excerpt is best understood as part of which broader context of the late twentieth century?

options.text: A worldwide turn toward free-market policies and reduced state economic roles
options.label: key
options.why: From the 1980s on, many governments, both capitalist and formerly communist, sold state enterprises and liberalized their economies. Russia's privatization belongs to this global trend.

options.text: A global wave of decolonization that created dozens of new states across Africa and Asia
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Decolonization happened mainly from the 1940s to the 1970s. It concerned political independence, not post-Soviet economic restructuring.

options.text: The expansion of government economic planning in response to the Great Depression of the 1930s
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Depression-era planning increased the state's economic role, so it comes from the wrong period and points in the opposite direction.

options.text: The spread of Green Revolution farming techniques that raised grain yields in developing nations
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Green Revolution was a real agricultural change in the twentieth century, but it has no connection to the ownership of Russian industry.

facts: Governments such as Margaret Thatcher's in Britain (1979-1990) privatized state industries in the 1980s.
After 1989-1991, former communist states in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union moved toward market economies.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt describes moving state enterprises into private ownership and selling shares for cash, which fits the global free-market turn.
design.evidence_quote: The next phase of the privatization program called for direct cash sales of shares in remaining state enterprises.

items.stem: The excerpt relies partly on figures from the organizers of the voucher system. This is most likely a limitation for historians because the organizers

options.text: had reason to present the program's results as a success
options.label: key
options.why: The figures for firms and workers come from 'the organizers of the voucher system.' The organizers ran the program, so they had an interest in reporting good results, and their numbers may need checking against other evidence.

options.text: were foreign advisers with no access to Russian economic records
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the excerpt or the credit line says the organizers were foreigners or lacked access to records.

options.text: opposed privatization and sought to exaggerate its failures
options.label: reversal
options.why: The organizers designed and ran the program, so any bias would favor it. The excerpt also reports successes, not failures.

options.text: wrote before the voucher program's first phase had actually begun
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The organizers report results from after the first phase was finished, so they cannot have written before it began.

facts: Russia's voucher privatization was run by the State Committee for the Management of State Property, headed by Anatoly Chubais, in the early 1990s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt credits its figures on 14,000 firms and two-thirds of the industrial workforce to the program's own organizers.
design.evidence_quote: According to the organizers of the voucher system, some 14,000 firms employing about two-thirds of the industrial labor force

items.stem: Which of the following was a development in another country in the late twentieth century that most closely resembles the policy described in the excerpt?

options.text: Britain's sale of state-owned firms such as British Telecom in the 1980s
options.label: key
options.why: Under Thatcher, Britain sold shares in state-owned companies to private investors. Like Russia's program, this transferred state enterprises to private hands and raised revenue for the government.

options.text: Mexico's nationalization of foreign-owned oil companies under President Cardenas in 1938
options.label: reversal
options.why: Mexico took private firms into state ownership, which is the opposite of privatization, and it did so decades earlier.

options.text: Cuba's seizure of foreign-owned sugar estates and businesses after the 1959 revolution
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Cuban revolutionary government nationalized private property, so its policy ran opposite to Russia's in the 1990s.

options.text: Egypt's nationalization of the Suez Canal Company under Gamal Abdel Nasser in 1956
options.label: reversal
options.why: Nasser moved a privately held company into state ownership, which reverses the direction described in the excerpt.

facts: British Telecom was privatized in 1984 under Margaret Thatcher.
Mexico nationalized its oil industry in 1938; Egypt nationalized the Suez Canal Company in 1956.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt describes selling shares in state enterprises for cash to finish privatization and raise government revenue, much like the British share sales.
design.evidence_quote: That phase would complete the transfer of state enterprises and would add to government revenues.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a similarity between the arguments in Source A and Source B about political authority?

options.text: Both hold that rightful political authority rests on agreement among people, not force.
options.label: key
options.why: Locke says no one can be subjected to political power without his own consent. Rousseau says force cannot make power legitimate and that the social order must be founded on conventions.

options.text: Both hold that hereditary monarchs receive their authority from God and must be obeyed without question.
options.label: reversal
options.why: This is divine-right theory, the very view both authors reject by grounding authority in consent or convention.

options.text: Both hold that humans in a state of nature lived in constant war, so only an absolute ruler can keep order.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This is the view of Thomas Hobbes. Locke here describes people in the state of nature as free, equal and independent.

options.text: Source A defends rule by a landed nobility, while Source B calls for the abolition of all private property.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Neither excerpt defends noble rule or calls for abolishing property. Locke treats secure property as one reason people form a community.

facts: Locke's Second Treatise (1690) argued that political society rests on the consent of free and equal individuals.
Rousseau's The Social Contract (1762) argued that legitimate authority rests on convention, not force or nature.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Locke requires consent, and Rousseau says the social order is founded on conventions, not on nature or force.
design.evidence_quote: this right does not come from nature, and must therefore be founded on conventions

items.stem: Which of the following arguments, made by some European writers in the 1600s and 1700s, would most directly challenge the claims in both sources?

options.text: Kings hold authority directly from God, not from any agreement among their subjects.
options.label: key
options.why: Divine-right theorists such as Robert Filmer and Bishop Bossuet said royal power came from God. That denies both Locke's consent and Rousseau's conventions as the basis of authority.

options.text: Governments are formed chiefly to protect the natural rights of life, liberty, and property of their members.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This restates Locke's own position, so it supports the sources and does not challenge them.

options.text: Sovereignty belongs to the nation as a whole, so laws should express the general will of its citizens.
options.label: reversal
options.why: This idea of popular sovereignty and the general will comes from Rousseau and supports, rather than refutes, the sources.

options.text: Free markets allocate goods better than state regulation, so governments should leave trade alone.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Laissez-faire economic thought, as in Adam Smith, deals with trade policy, not with where political legitimacy comes from.

facts: Robert Filmer's Patriarcha (published 1680) defended the divine and patriarchal right of kings, and Locke's First Treatise was written to refute it.
Bishop Jacques-Benigne Bossuet defended divine-right absolutism under Louis XIV in the late 1600s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Both sources deny that authority comes from nature or force and root it in consent, so a theory of authority given by God would contradict them.
design.evidence_quote: no one can be put out of this estate, and subjected to the political power of another, without his own consent

items.stem: Which of the following developments in England most directly provided the historical context for Source A?

options.text: Parliament's struggles with Stuart kings, ending in the Glorious Revolution of 1688
options.label: key
options.why: The Two Treatises were published in 1689-1690, just after Parliament replaced James II with William and Mary. Locke's theory of consent was used to justify that change of rulers.

options.text: The Chartist movement's mass petitions demanding universal male suffrage and secret ballots
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Chartism took place in the 1830s and 1840s, about 150 years after Locke wrote.

options.text: The rise of steam-powered textile factories and the workers' protests they provoked in the cities
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Factory industrialization began in the late 1700s, long after the 1690 publication.

options.text: The break with the Roman Catholic Church under Henry VIII and the founding of the Church of England
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The English Reformation under Henry VIII happened in the 1530s, more than a century before Locke's work.

facts: In the Glorious Revolution of 1688-1689, Parliament replaced James II with William III and Mary II.
The English Bill of Rights of 1689 limited royal power.
Locke's Two Treatises of Government were published in 1689-1690.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line dates Locke's English work to 1689-1690, the years of the Glorious Revolution.

items.stem: Ideas such as those in both sources most directly influenced which of the following developments in the period 1750 to 1900?

options.text: Creole leaders' arguments justifying independence from Spanish rule in South America
options.label: key
options.why: Leaders such as Simon Bolivar drew on Enlightenment ideas of popular sovereignty and consent to argue against Spanish colonial rule in the 1810s and 1820s.

options.text: The Meiji constitution of 1889, which declared the emperor sacred and the source of sovereignty
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Meiji constitution placed sovereignty in the emperor rather than in the consent of the people, so it reflects the opposite principle.

options.text: The Qing Self-Strengthening Movement's effort to adopt Western arms while preserving Confucian rule
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Self-strengthening borrowed Western technology while rejecting political change. It was not based on theories of consent.

options.text: British factory legislation limiting the working hours of children employed in textile mills
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Factory Acts responded to industrial working conditions, not to debates about where political authority comes from.

facts: Spanish American independence movements led by creoles such as Simon Bolivar won independence in the 1810s and 1820s.
Bolivar's Jamaica Letter (1815) drew on Enlightenment political ideas.
The Meiji constitution of 1889 vested sovereignty in the emperor.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Both sources argue that authority imposed without consent is illegitimate, and revolutionaries in the Americas used this idea to justify independence.
design.evidence_quote: as soon as it can shake off the yoke, and shakes it off, it does still better

items.stem: In Source B, Rousseau's reasoning about force most directly suggests which of the following?

options.text: Rule imposed by force alone can be rightfully overturned when people are able to do so
options.label: key
options.why: Rousseau argues that if force were the only basis of power, a people that shakes off the yoke regains its liberty by the same right that took it away.

options.text: A people compelled to obey must always submit, since resistance destroys the sacred social order
options.label: reversal
options.why: Rousseau says a people that shakes off the yoke does even better. He calls the social order sacred only because it rests on convention, not on force.

options.text: Rousseau can trace exactly how humans lost their natural freedom and fell under the rule of masters
options.label: reversal
options.why: Rousseau says plainly that he does not know how this change came about. He claims only to explain what could make it legitimate.

options.text: Nature itself assigns some people to rule and others to obey, giving force a lasting legitimacy
options.label: reversal
options.why: Rousseau states that the right to social order does not come from nature.

facts: Rousseau's The Social Contract (1762) argued that might does not make right and that legitimate authority requires a social compact.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Rousseau's hypothetical argument about force concludes that a people regains its liberty by the same right that took it away.
design.evidence_quote: regaining its liberty by the same right as took it away

items.stem: The arguments in both sources are best understood as part of which broader intellectual development?

options.text: Enlightenment use of reason to question traditional sources of political authority
options.label: key
options.why: Locke and Rousseau were leading Enlightenment thinkers. They reasoned about natural liberty and consent to test whether existing authority was legitimate.

options.text: Social Darwinist theories applying natural selection to rank societies and justify empire
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Social Darwinism arose in the later 1800s, after Darwin's 1859 work, long after both texts were written.

options.text: Marxist analysis of history as class struggle leading to a workers' revolution against capital
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Marx and Engels published The Communist Manifesto in 1848, well after both sources.

options.text: Neo-Confucian teaching that subjects owe loyalty to rulers just as children owe obedience to parents
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Neo-Confucianism was an East Asian tradition that stressed hierarchical duty, not consent among free and equal individuals.

facts: Locke (1690) and Rousseau (1762) are central figures of the European Enlightenment.
Marx and Engels published The Communist Manifesto in 1848.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Both authors reason from the natural freedom of humans to the conditions under which authority becomes legitimate, which is typical of Enlightenment political thought.
design.evidence_quote: Man is born free; and everywhere he is in chains.
